title: Embed or reference
summary: Which side of a relationship goes inside the document and which one gets a link, and what each answer charges you on every read and every write.

sources.author: MongoDB
sources.title: Best Practices for Data Modeling in MongoDB

cards.front: An order's line items, and a product's reviews. Same shape of relationship, opposite answers. Which is which, and why?
cards.back: Items embed, reviews reference. Items are written once with the order and bounded by it; reviews arrive at their own times and nothing stops them growing.

cards.front: Two pieces of data have to commit or fail as one. What does that decide about the boundary between them?
cards.back: That they want to be one document. An operation on a single document is atomic, so keeping them together removes the need for a transaction.

cards.front: An embedded array has reached 40,000 entries and the page shows ten of them. Name the two costs, and the ceiling you are heading for.
cards.back: Every read reads the whole document and every edit rewrites it, so ten reviews cost forty thousand. The ceiling is the 16MB BSON document size limit.

cards.front: An order carries the customer's name, copied at checkout. The customer changes it. Which reading makes the old orders correct?
cards.back: That the field is a snapshot of the name at the order, and the field name should say so. Read as a cache of the current name, every rename owes a write to every order that copied it.

cards.front: What do you have to know before designing a DynamoDB schema that you can postpone when designing for an RDBMS?
cards.back: The questions it will have to answer: AWS says not to start a DynamoDB design until you know the query patterns. A relational model can be normalized first and extended later.

cards.front: You reach for a Postgres `jsonb` column instead of columns. What does it not preserve?
cards.back: Key order, duplicate keys, and whitespace: it stores a decomposed binary format rather than your text, and where a key repeats only the last value is kept.

cards.front: The child is queried on its own, by screens that never load the parent. Does that argue for embedding or referencing?
cards.back: Referencing: the child can exist without a parent. Embedded, every one of those screens loads a parent it does not want.
